title: Syllables and pronunciation traditions

objectives.can: Divide a Greek word into syllables, find its stressed syllable, and read a verse aloud in one consistent pronunciation.

explanation.summary: A Greek word has as many syllables as it has vowels or diphthongs, and its accent shows the syllable that carries the stress. Greek can be read aloud in several traditions of pronunciation. The choice never changes a spelling, a word or its grammar, but within one reading you must keep to a single tradition.

sections.heading: Counting syllables
body: A syllable has one vowel or one diphthong. So the number of syllables in a word is the number of its vowels and diphthongs, counted as one each. λόγος has two syllables, ἄνθρωπος has three and κατέλαβεν has four. A word such as καί, which is one diphthong with a consonant, is a single syllable; so is φῶς.
Two vowels side by side that are not a diphthong are two syllables. The ω and η of ζωή are separate, so ζωή has two syllables. The two dots of a diaeresis show the same thing.

sections.heading: Dividing a word
body: Reading rules for dividing a word: a single consonant between two vowels goes with the vowel after it (λό-γος, ἐ-γέ-νε-το). Two consonants that are alike are split (Ἰ-ω-άν-νης). A group of consonants that can begin a Greek word goes with the vowel after it (σκο-τί-α, ἄν-θρω-πος); a group that cannot begin a word is split (ἀρ-χή).
These are rules of convenience for reading and for printing a word across two lines. They do not change the pronunciation.

sections.heading: Which syllable has the stress
body: The last syllable of a word is called the ultima, the one before it the penult, and the one before that the antepenult. An accent can stand only on one of these three. In ἄνθρωπος the accent is on the antepenult, in λόγος on the penult and in ἀρχῇ on the ultima.

In the school convention the syllable with the accent is read with stress, a little louder and longer than the others. Some teachers instead stress by the Latin rule, the penult when it is long. Whichever you use, use it consistently.

sections.heading: Three traditions of pronunciation
body: No one pronunciation of Greek is the only correct one, and the table of this lesson sets three side by side. The Erasmian pronunciation, named after Erasmus, who proposed it in the sixteenth century, is a teaching convention. It keeps every letter and every diphthong distinct, which is convenient for learning, and it is the one used for the sounds in G0.1.1 and G0.2.1. The reconstructed Koine is what scholars infer for Greek of the Roman period from spelling mistakes in papyri, inscriptions and ancient descriptions of sounds; it varied from place to place and changed over the centuries, so the table gives two values where scholars differ. Modern or ecclesiastical Greek is the pronunciation of Greek speakers today, and it is the one used when the Greek Orthodox Church reads the New Testament aloud.

The choice changes no spelling. ἦν is written ἦν whether it is read 'ayn' (Erasmian) or 'een' (modern). It is the same word with the same meaning and the same grammar. The only requirement is consistency: do not read one word the Erasmian way and the next the modern way.
In the strict Erasmian system, θ, φ and χ were a t, p and k followed by a puff of breath, and most courses simplify them to th, ph and ch as in the school convention.

sections.heading: Reading a verse aloud
body: To read a verse in one tradition, follow three steps. First, choose the tradition. Second, read each word letter by letter, giving each letter and diphthong the value from that tradition's column. Third, stress the syllable that carries the accent. The phrase ἦν ὁ λόγος is 'ayn ho LO-gos' in the Erasmian pronunciation and 'een o LO-ghos' in the modern. The rough breathing of ὁ is sounded in the first and silent in the second.

misunderstandings: The three pronunciations are not three spellings. The Greek letters are the same in every tradition; only the sounds given to them differ.
The Erasmian pronunciation is a teaching convention, not a recording of how Greek was spoken at any one time or place.
'Modern' does not mean 'wrong' for the New Testament. It is the continuous living pronunciation of the language and is used in worship today.
Do not mix traditions in a single reading. 'een ho LO-gos' takes the modern ἦν with the Erasmian rough breathing.
A syllable is not a letter. Count vowels and diphthongs, not letters.

deeper.heading: A sixteenth-century quarrel
body: When Greek was revived in Western Europe, scholars first learned it from Greek teachers, who taught the modern pronunciation, in which several different letters sound alike. Erasmus argued in 1528 that ancient Greek must have kept these letters distinct, and proposed the system that now bears his name. The argument was about sounds only; no one proposed changing the written text.

examples.analysis: Three words with three stress positions. ἀρχῇ has two syllables, ἀρ-χῇ, with the circumflex on the last. λόγος has two, λό-γος, with the acute on the next to last. θεόν has two, θε-όν: the ε and ο are separate vowels, not a diphthong, and the acute is on the last. In the Erasmian pronunciation they are read 'ar-KHAY', 'LO-gos' and 'the-ON'; in the modern, 'ar-KHEE', 'LO-ghos' and 'the-ON'.

examples.analysis: ζωή (here written ζωὴ) has two syllables, ζω-ή, because ω and η are two vowels and not a diphthong. ἀνθρώπων has three, ἀν-θρώ-πων: νθ cannot begin a word and is split, while θρ can and goes with the next vowel. The accent is on the next to last, the long ω.

examples.analysis: πάντα has two syllables with the accent on the first, the next to last. αὐτοῦ has two, αὐ-τοῦ: αυ and ου are diphthongs, one syllable each. ἐγένετο has four syllables, ἐ-γέ-νε-το, and its accent falls on the third from last.

examples.analysis: φαίνει has two syllables, φαί-νει, both with a diphthong. In the Erasmian pronunciation it is 'PHAI-nei'. The modern pronunciation is 'FE-nee', because αι is read e, ει is read ee and φ is read f. The spelling is the same in both. κατέλαβεν has four syllables, κα-τέ-λα-βεν, with the accent on the third from last.
